title: Christians are the salt that preserves the world
source_text: Ἀλλ᾿ οἱ καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν Κέλσου πάντες ἂν πεισθέντες Ῥωμαῖοι εὐχόμενοι περιέσονται τῶν πολεμίων ἢ οὐδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν πολεμήσονται. φρουρούμενοι ὑπὸ θείας δυνάμεως, τῆς διὰ πεντήκοντα δικαίους πέντε πόλεις ὅλας ἐπαγγειλαμένης διασῶσαι. ἅλες γὰρ εἰσι τηρητικοὶ τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς συστάσεων τοῦ κόσμου οἱ τοῦ θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι, καὶ συνέστηκε τὰ ἐπὶ γῆς, ὅσον οἱ ἅλες οὐ τρέπονται· „ἐὰν γὰρ τὸ ἅλας μωρανθῇ,“ „οὔτ᾿ εἰς γῆν οὔτ᾿ εἰς κόπρον“ „ἰσχύει ἔτι“ ἀλλὰ „βληθὲν ἔξω“ καταπατηθήσεται „ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων.“ „ὁ δ᾿ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκουέτω,“ πῶς ταῦτα λέγεται. καὶ ἡμεῖς δὲ, ὅτε μὲν ἐπιτρέπει ὁ θεὸς τῷ πειράζοντι δοὺς ἐξουσίαν τὴν τοῦ διώκειν ἡμᾶς, διωκόμεθα· ὅτε δ᾿ ὁ θεὸς (οὐ) βούλεται τοῦθ᾿ ἡμᾶς πάσχειν, καὶ ἐν μισοῦντι ἡμᾶς τῷ κόσμῳ παραδόξως εἰρήνην ἄγομεν καὶ θαῤῥοῦμεν ἐπὶ τῷ εἰπόντι· „θαρσεῖτε, ἐγὼ νενίκηκα τὸν κόσμον.“ καὶ ἀληθῶς νενίκηκε „τὸν κόσμον,“ διόπερ (ἰσχύει ὁ κόσμος) εἰς ὅσον νικήσας αὐτὸν βούλεται, λαβὼν ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς τὸ νικᾶν „τὸν κόσμον·“ θαῤῥοῦμεν δὲ τῇ ἐκείνου νίκῃ. εἰ δὲ βούλεται πάλιν ἡμᾶς ἀθλεῖν καὶ ἀγωνίζεσθαι περὶ εὐσεβείας, ἡκέτωσαν ἀνταγωνισταὶ, πρὸς οὓς ἐροῦμεν· „πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.“ καὶ γὰρ δύο στρουθίων πιπρασκομένων, ὡς ὠνόμασεν ἡ γραφὴ, „ἀσσαρίου,“ „ἓν εἰς παγίδα οὐ πίπτει ἄνευ τοῦ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς πατρός.“ καὶ ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον πάντα ἡ θεία περιείληφε πρόνοια, ὡς μηδὲ τὰς τρίχας „τῆς κεφαλῆς“ ἡμῶν ἐκπεφευγέναι τὸ ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἠριθμῆσθαι.
pass_a_gloss: But those who on Celsus's hypothesis, all the Romans, if persuaded (πεισθέντες), praying (εὔχομαι) will overcome (περίειμι) their enemies (πολέμιοι), or will not even at all (τὴν ἀρχήν) make war (πολεμέω), being guarded (φρουρέω) by divine power (θεία δύναμις), which promised (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) to save (διασῴζω) five whole cities through fifty righteous (δίκαιοι). For the men of God are salts (ἅλες) preserving (τηρητικός) the structures/compositions (συστάσεις) of the world (κόσμος) on earth, and the things on earth hold together (συνίστημι) as long as the salts are not turned/spoiled (τρέπομαι). 'For if the salt has become foolish/tasteless (μωραίνω)', 'neither for earth nor for dung (κόπρος)' 'is it strong/fit (ἰσχύω) still', but 'having been thrown (βάλλω) out' will be trampled (καταπατέω) 'by men'. 'He who has ears let him hear', how these things are said. And we too, when God permits (ἐπιτρέπω) the tempter (ὁ πειράζων), giving (him) authority (ἐξουσία) to persecute (διώκω) us, are persecuted; but when God (does not) wish us to suffer (πάσχω) this, even in the world hating (μισέω) us, paradoxically (παραδόξως) we keep peace (εἰρήνην ἄγω) and are confident (θαρρέω) in the one who said: 'Be of good courage (θαρσεῖτε), I have conquered (νικάω) the world.' And truly he has conquered 'the world', wherefore (the world has power (ἰσχύω)) as far as he who conquered it wishes, having received from the Father the conquering of 'the world'; and we are confident in his victory (νίκη). But if he wishes us again to compete (ἀθλέω) and struggle (ἀγωνίζομαι) for piety (εὐσέβεια), let opponents (ἀνταγωνισταί) come, to whom we will say: 'I am strong for (ἰσχύω) all things in the one empowering (ἐνδυναμόω) me, Christ Jesus our Lord.' For of two sparrows (στρουθίον) being sold, as Scripture named (ὀνομάζω) it, 'for an assarion (ἀσσάριον)', 'one does not fall into a snare (παγίς) without the Father in the heavens.' And to such an extent divine providence (θεία πρόνοια) has encompassed (περιλαμβάνω) all things, that not even the hairs 'of the head' of ours have escaped (ἐκφεύγω) being numbered (ἀριθμέω) by it/him.
pass_b_english: But on Celsus’s supposition, if all the Romans were persuaded, by praying they will overcome their enemies, or they will not even make war at all, guarded by the divine power which promised to save five whole cities for the sake of fifty righteous men (compare Genesis 18:24–26). For the men of God are salt that preserves the order of the world on earth, and the things on earth hold together as long as the salt does not go bad. For “if the salt has lost its taste,” it “is no longer fit either for the soil or for the dunghill,” but “is thrown out” and will be trampled “by men” (Matthew 5:13; Luke 14:34–35). “He who has ears, let him hear” (Luke 14:35) how these things are said.

We too, when God allows the tempter and gives him authority to persecute us, are persecuted; but when God does not wish us to suffer this, even in a world that hates us (compare John 15:18) we live in peace, against all expectation, and take courage from Him who said: “Take courage, I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). And truly He has overcome “the world”; therefore the world has power only so far as He who overcame it wills, since He received from the Father the power to overcome “the world.” And we take courage from His victory.

But if He wishes us once more to contend and struggle for piety, let the adversaries come, and we will say to them: “I can do all things in Him who strengthens me, Christ Jesus our Lord” (Philippians 4:13; 1 Timothy 1:12). For when two sparrows are sold “for a penny,” as Scripture names the price, “not one falls into a snare without the Father in heaven” (Matthew 10:29). And divine providence has embraced all things so fully that not even the hairs “of our head” have escaped being numbered by Him (Matthew 10:30).

choices.choice: ‘Five whole cities’ for fifty righteous: Genesis 18:24-26 speaks of sparing Sodom (the ‘place’) for fifty; the five cities of the plain are those of Genesis 14:2 (compare Wisdom 10:6, ‘the Five Cities’); Origen combines them; cited as ‘compare’. The salt saying conflates Matthew 5:13 (μωρανθῇ; εἰς οὐδὲν ἰσχύει ἔτι εἰ μὴ βληθὲν ἔξω καταπατεῖσθαι ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων) and Luke 14:34-35 (οὔτε εἰς γῆν οὔτε εἰς κοπρίαν; ὁ ἔχων ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω). ‘the order of the world on earth’ renders τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς συστάσεων τοῦ κόσμου. The negative in ‘ὅτε δ᾿ ὁ θεὸς (οὐ) βούλεται’ is an editorial supplement (Koetschau), required by the sense and followed here. ’(ἰσχύει ὁ κόσμος)’ is also an editorial supplement, followed (‘the world has power only so far as He ... wills’). ‘a world that hates us’ alludes to John 15:18-19 (compare John 17:14). The Philippians quotation is completed with the wording of 1 Timothy 1:12 (‘Christ Jesus our Lord, who strengthened me’). Matthew 10:29 reads ‘shall not fall to the ground without your Father’; Origen has ‘into a snare’ and ‘the Father in heaven’ (the snare perhaps from Amos 3:5; uncertain, not cited inline). ἀσσάριον rendered ‘penny’; ‘as Scripture names the price’ renders ὡς ὠνόμασεν ἡ γραφή. ‘when two sparrows are sold’ renders the genitive absolute δύο στρουθίων πιπρασκομένων. The final ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ (‘by Him’) may refer to God or to providence; rendered ‘by Him’. Celsus’s quoted words do not occur in this chapter; ‘on Celsus’s supposition’ renders καθ᾿ ὑπόθεσιν Κέλσου.
'For though two sparrows are sold' -> 'For when two sparrows are sold' (genitive absolute, no concession in the Greek)

Genesis 18:24-26, Matthew 5:13, Luke 14:34-35, John 15:18, John 16:33, Philippians 4:13, 1 Timothy 1:12, Matthew 10:29-30 checked: correct; editorial supplements (οὐ), (ἰσχύει ὁ κόσμος) followed and noted
